title: Four marks
hook: the church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, each tradition explaining how

segments.voice: Yesterday, tongues, and three answers from one Bible. Your line was the spirit blows. What curious question did you ask instead of deciding? Day one thousand ninety-six.

This Sunday, in a Catholic parish, an Orthodox cathedral and an Anglican chapel, people will stand up and say the same old sentence from the Nicene Creed. It describes the church with four words: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Then, after the service, they'll go home to churches that are plainly not one, that are sometimes not holy, that are very local, and that argue about what the apostles meant. So what are they saying? A wish? A boast? A promise? These four words are called the marks of the church: the signs by which you're meant to recognize it. And the churches that say them each explain them their own way. Today's words: four marks.
screen: `A WISH, A BOAST, OR A PROMISE?`

segments.voice: Take them one at a time. One. Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the King James: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism." And in John's Gospel Jesus prays "That they all may be one." Holy. Not because its members are spotless, but because it belongs to God, set apart, the way we said a few days ago. Catholic, with a small c. It means universal, for the whole: every place, every people, the whole faith. Apostolic. Paul says the household of God is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone." Now the different explanations, side by side. The Catholic Church teaches that the one church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, apostolic through bishops in succession from the apostles, in communion with the pope, while recognizing real elements of the church beyond its walls. The Orthodox Church holds that it is the one church, kept apostolic by bishops who guard the faith handed down. Anglicans also keep bishops in succession and see themselves within the one catholic church. Protestant confessions like Augsburg find the church wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly given; apostolic, for them, means teaching what the apostles taught. So the same four words can describe a visible body with a shape and a history, or a fellowship of believers spread through many churches. One thing these explanations can share: the four marks are said as faith, not as a report card. Christians say them on days when their own church looks nothing like them.
screen: `ONE BODY, ONE LORD, ONE BAPTISM.` · `HOLY: BELONGING TO GOD.` · `CATHOLIC: FOR THE WHOLE.` · `APOSTOLIC: BUILT ON THE APOSTLES.` · then, large: `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC, APOSTOLIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for one mark in your church. Settle, and breathe slowly. If you belong to a church, bring it to mind: the building, the faces, the arguments. Run the four words past it. One. Holy. Catholic. Apostolic. Which one feels thinnest right now? Maybe it's divided. Maybe it's turned inward and forgotten the whole world. Pick that mark. If you pray, you can ask for it, for your church, by name. If you don't belong to a church, try the same with any community you're part of: a family, a team, a neighborhood. Which of those marks would it most need? The bell holds the time.
Four marks. One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the signs of the church in the Nicene Creed, said together, explained differently.
Your line: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Today, do one small thing for the mark you picked: a call across a divide, a look outward, a word from the old faith. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches confess the church as one, holy, catholic and apostolic in the Nicene Creed, often aloud together at the Eucharist; each tradition explains the marks in its own way.

myth: "catholic" in the creed means only the Roman Catholic Church
with a small c it means universal, for the whole. churches across traditions say it.
"holy" means the church's members are spotless
the church is holy because it belongs to God, set apart, not because its members never fail.
Protestant confessions like Augsburg tie the church to the preached gospel and the sacraments
they find the church wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly given.

fork.setup: you say "one, holy, catholic, apostolic" on Sunday, but your church is split and struggling. what are you doing?
options: lying, so better to stop saying it.
confessing faith in what the church is in God's eyes and is called to be.
fork.reveal: the marks are said as faith, not a report card. traditions explain them differently, but none says them only on good days.

original.note: Greek: universal, for the whole — the word behind "catholic" in the creed.

trapdoor: what you thought: four marks are grades a church gets.
what it means: one, holy, catholic and apostolic are the creed's signs of the church, explained differently by Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Protestants.
what a scholar hears: the marks come from the Nicene Creed's line on the church; Lumen Gentium 8 and the Augsburg Confession, Article 7, explain them differently.

notes: The phrase 'one, holy, catholic and apostolic' is a paraphrase of the creed's line; the BCP 1662 text omits 'holy' ('one Catholick and Apostolick Church'), so no translation is quoted.
Some free-church and Baptist congregations do not recite creeds; the hook says 'the churches that say them'.

Catholic summary paraphrases Lumen Gentium 8 ('subsists in') and its recognition of elements of sanctification and truth outside its visible structure. Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant (Augsburg VII) summaries: confirm fairness.
'Catholic ... means universal, for the whole' is a definitional gloss; the derivation from καθ' ὅλου appears in the trapdoor only. Confirm.
Hook's picture of Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican congregations saying the creed on Sunday: confirm phrasing.
Editor pass: cut the stock 'here's the twist'; softened 'these explanations share' to 'can share'; removed the katholikos/kath' holou etymology from the trapdoor under the claims rule.
Audit (2026-10-02): cut the narrator's self-referential 'none of them gets ranked here'; the explanations are simply set side by side.
